content: Tinea corporis, also referred to as ringworm, tinea circinata, or tinea glabrosa, is a superficial fungal infection (dermatophytosis) that primarily affects the arms and legs, particularly on smooth, hairless skin. However, it can occur on any part of the body. The infection can present with various appearances, but the most recognizable feature is the presence of enlarging, raised, red rings with a central area of clearing, which is characteristic of ringworm. Similar lesions can also appear on the scalp (tinea capitis), the beard area (tinea barbae), or the groin (tinea cruris, commonly known as jock itch or dhobi itch). Other classic features of tinea corporis include: The edges of the rash are elevated and feel scaly to the touch. The surrounding skin may sometimes appear dry and flaky. Hair loss is almost always observed in the areas affected by the infection. Tinea corporis is caused by dermatophytes, a type of fungus that resides on the superficial layers of the skin. Under favorable conditions, these fungi can cause a rash or infection. The disease is often transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact with an infected individual. It can also spread from animals to humans, as pets like dogs and cats frequently harbor the fungus. Other animals, such as horses, pigs, ferrets, and cows, can also be sources of infection. Additionally, the fungus can be transmitted via contaminated objects, such as personal care items, bed linens, combs, athletic gear, or hairbrushes. Certain individuals are at higher risk of acquiring tinea corporis, including those who: Live in crowded, humid environments. Sweat excessively, as sweat creates a moist environment conducive to fungal growth, particularly in areas like the armpits, groin, and skin folds of the abdomen. Participate in close-contact sports such as soccer, rugby, or wrestling. Wear tight, poorly ventilated clothing. Have compromised immune systems, such as individuals with HIV or those taking immunosuppressive medications. When a fungal infection is suspected, a physician will examine the skin and collect scrapings from the affected area. These skin scrapings are examined under a microscope to confirm the presence of a fungus. If the initial microscopic examination is inconclusive, the scrapings may be sent for fungal culture, which can take several days to yield results due to the slow growth of the fungus. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) tests are another diagnostic method commonly used. Preventing tinea corporis involves maintaining dry skin and avoiding contact with infectious materials, as fungi thrive in warm, moist environments. Preventive measures include: Washing hands after handling animals, soil, or plants. Avoiding direct contact with lesions on infected individuals. Wearing loose-fitting clothing. Practicing good hygiene, especially when engaging in sports involving physical contact. Treatment for tinea corporis typically involves the application of topical antifungal creams to the affected skin. In more extensive or difficult-to-treat cases, systemic treatment with oral antifungal medications may be necessary. Topical antifungals are applied to the lesion twice daily for at least three weeks. While the lesion often resolves within two weeks, treatment should continue for an additional week to ensure complete eradication of the fungus. Commonly used topical antifungals include clotrimazole, ketoconazole, miconazole, terbinafine, tolnaftate, and butenafine. For cases involving multiple lesions, extensive involvement, secondary infections, or immunocompromised patients, oral antifungal medications may be prescribed. These are typically taken once daily for seven days and are associated with higher clinical cure rates. Commonly used oral antifungals include itraconazole and terbinafine. Tinea corporis is moderately contagious and can affect both humans and animals. Proper measures should be taken to prevent its spread. Children, in particular, should be educated about the infection and its prevention, including avoiding skin-to-skin contact with infected individuals or animals, wearing breathable clothing, and not sharing towels, clothing, or combs. If pets are present in the household, they should be examined for tinea, especially if they exhibit patchy hair loss or excessive scratching. Although tinea corporis can be uncomfortable, it is easily treatable and preventable in individuals with a healthy immune system.
